clue.text: In which fortune rarely favours the brave

definitions.text: In which fortune rarely favours the brave

parts.words: In which fortune rarely favours the brave
parts.note: a playful inversion of the proverb: in cowboy films the bold hero always wins, so the claim that fortune rarely favours the brave is a wry joke about a film genre

explanation.surface: A gloomy observation about some world where courage goes unrewarded.
explanation.definitionFit: Cowboy films set on the American frontier form a genre in which, contrary to the clue's tease, the brave gunslinger nearly always triumphs.

clue.text: Indians jump over one

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over the second

parts.note: to jump is to hop
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Some people leap over a single obstacle.
explanation.definitionFit: A Native American people of Arizona, once commonly called Indians.

clue.text: Kiss when departing county existence

indicators.note: the kiss is leaving the county's name, so its letter is removed

parts.note: Essex is an English county east of London
X is the conventional symbol for a kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A farewell kiss as someone leaves the county they lived in.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking X from ESSEX, an English county, leaves the Latin philosophical term for being.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'to be', used in philosophy to mean being or essential nature.

clue.text: Needing drink, first of ales free

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word ales is taken

parts.note: to free something of a thing is to rid it

explanation.surface: A thirsty drinker grabs the first of the beers being given away for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Parched and dry, the state of something or someone in want of water.

clue.text: Topic interest then dissipates for Tom, Dick and Harry

parts.note: a topic is a theme

indicators.note: the letters scatter and regroup, as something dissipated breaks up

explanation.surface: Someone's interest in a subject fades away, for a trio of named men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dissipates' signals the anagram; 'for' is a link. The phrase is usually singular, the man in the street, made plural for the puzzle's men-and-boys theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Every Tom, Dick and Harry is an idiom for ordinary people at large, the average citizen.

clue.text: Lawkeepers have been — by loutish roughs

indicators.note: roughs up suggests manhandling, so the letters of the words before are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Police officers have been assaulted by thuggish hooligans.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash is just punctuation; 'roughs' rearranges BEEN BY LOUTISH, all thirteen letters, into the whole four-word phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A familiar nickname for police officers, from the colour of their uniforms.

clue.text: Mock bone china for 2 at 4?

parts.note: to mock someone is to tease them
a T-bone gives the letter T for bone

explanation.surface: Imitation porcelain set out for a couple at four o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: '2 at 4' is two people at four o'clock, the traditional British afternoon tea hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Cups, saucers and pot in matching porcelain, laid out for afternoon refreshments.

clue.text: Take my picture over there instead

definitions.text: Take my picture over there instead

parts.words: Take my picture over there instead
parts.note: reads like a request to a photographer, but means move a painting on the wall to a different spot

explanation.surface: Someone asks a photographer to snap them from a different position.
explanation.definitionFit: To put a painting up again somewhere else on the walls.

clue.text: Presumably, everyone is staying? Not I!

definitions.meaning: if nobody departs, then all must be remaining
the philosophical term for whatever is outside the self

explanation.surface: A host checks whether all guests are staying; one declines.
explanation.definitionFit: If not one person leaves, then all remain; and in philosophy the not-self is everything outside the I.

clue.text: Go downhill fast

parts.note: sounds like rapid decline or deterioration, but means speeding down a snowy slope

explanation.surface: Something deteriorating rapidly.
explanation.definitionFit: To glide down a snowy mountainside on long runners, often at speed.

clue.text: Source of mineral making an awful mint in auction

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are placed inside the sale

parts.note: an auction is a sale

indicators.note: an awful version of the word mint is a mangled one, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone makes a terrible fortune at an auction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' looks like an adjective on the fortune, but it signals rearranging the coin-maker's word; 'making an' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: An underground excavation where sodium chloride is dug out.

clue.text: This might follow major in smashing tile

indicators.note: the small word smashes into the middle of the longer one

parts.note: major-domo is a head steward, so domo might follow major
taken as written

explanation.surface: A game piece smashed in some major event.
explanation.walkthrough: A major-domo is the chief steward of a large household, so the second half of that compound is what might follow major.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the small spotted oblong pieces used in a game where they are laid end to end.

clue.text: Woman enclosing area to take on board

parts.note: her refers to a woman

explanation.surface: A woman fences in a patch of land to bring something aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: To take on board an idea is to listen to and absorb it.

clue.text: Very sharp weapon, say, lost

indicators.note: the abbreviation goes missing from the weapon's name

parts.note: an assegai is a slender iron-tipped spear of southern Africa
say means for example, abbreviated EG

explanation.surface: An extremely keen blade, for instance, has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: ASSEGAI loses EG ('say', as in for example).
explanation.definitionFit: A musical direction from Italian meaning extremely, as in allegro assai.

clue.text: Horrify, taking drug from it?

indicators.note: taking the drug from the word means removing its letter

parts.note: it is sex appeal, charm
E is short for ecstasy, a drug

explanation.surface: Someone is horrified at the idea of removing drugs from somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' means sex appeal, as in the It girl; remove E (ecstasy) from APPEAL; 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To shock or dismay someone deeply.

clue.text: 17 deals effectively with more than one company, as 5 from 6 Across

definitions.text: deals effectively with more than one company, as 5 from 6 Across
definitions.meaning: the idiom about distinguishing grown men from boys: the experienced from the novices

explanation.surface: Some company handles several firms well, telling men from boys.
explanation.definitionFit: To divide things into groups, and the idiom about telling adults from youngsters uses this verb.

clue.text: See 5
Cause pain to a snake

parts.note: to nag is to pester, causing pain or irritation

explanation.surface: Hurting a serpent.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu and Buddhist myth a serpent deity, often depicted as a cobra.

clue.text: 14 record a speed on board, as 5 from 6 Across?

indicators.note: on board means inside a steamship, so the pieces go inside

parts.note: board as in on board a ship, the steamship abbreviation SS
an EP is an extended-play record
a rate is a speed

explanation.surface: Someone logs a speed aboard a vessel, sorting adults from boys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as 5 from 6 Across' points to separating the men from the boys, the puzzle's theme; 14 and 17 define each other.
explanation.definitionFit: To divide or tell apart, as answer 14 does.

clue.text: Type lacking, basically?

parts.note: a font that lacks the little strokes at the base of letters; basically means at the base

explanation.surface: Someone missing a certain personality type at heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A typeface without the small finishing strokes at the ends of letters.

clue.text: See 6
See 5
Goals changed at half time

parts.note: in football, teams switch which side of the pitch they attack at the interval

explanation.surface: A football team's targets shifted during the break.
explanation.definitionFit: The two halves of the pitch, each with a goal, which teams swap after the interval.

clue.text: Rotten American raised in the East End

definitions.text: American raised in the East End

explanation.surface: A rotten American brought up in London's East End.
explanation.definitionFit: Infected or putrid; and in Cockney rhyming slang a tank of sewage rhymes with Yank, an American.

clue.text: Fabric of vehicle-free Cumbrian city

indicators.note: free of the vehicle means without it, so those letters are removed

parts.note: Carlisle is the county town of Cumbria, in north-west England
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Cloth from a northern English city where traffic is banned.
explanation.definitionFit: A smooth, tightly twisted cotton thread used for stockings.

clue.text: After taking roundabout, one races clear

indicators.note: after taking away the circle, the number word loses that letter

parts.note: taken as written
a roundabout is circular, like the letter O
the TT races are motorbike races on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A driver takes a roundabout, and someone speeds off into open road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roundabout' stands for the circular letter, removed as 'After taking' says; the Isle of Man TT is a famous motorcycle race.
explanation.definitionFit: To clear a sum is to earn it after deductions, the British spelling of net.

clue.text: Ran for Union status

parts.note: sounds like standing for election in a students' union, but means running away to marry

explanation.surface: A student stood for office in the Union.
explanation.definitionFit: Ran off secretly to get married, seeking the union of wedlock.

clue.text: Some getting to Miss World is how to outwit good-looker

indicators.note: only some of the letters of these words are taken, running across them

explanation.surface: Advice on how to beat a beauty queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' picks letters out of WORLD IS HOW.
explanation.definitionFit: An attractive person, informally a dish.

clue.text: That bloke's Terry, bursting bubbles in West Ham?

indicators.note: the actress's name bursts into the middle of the pronoun phrase

parts.note: that bloke is becomes he's
Ellen Terry was a celebrated Victorian actress

explanation.surface: A man named Terry popping soap bubbles at a London football ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang: bubble and squeak = Greek, and West Ham is in east London; ELLEN goes into HE'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Greeks, as named in their own language; Cockney slang turns them into bubbles.

clue.text: Port unfinished at a dance

indicators.note: the port's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Hull is a port in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A port city left incomplete at a ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hawaiian dance with swaying hips.

clue.text: Sail close to the wind

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Sail close to the wind', has no count and is cut short: the blog shows the answer hidden in 'bluffing', a word missing from the held clue.

clue.text: Red letters?

parts.note: letters printed in red, but really letters standing for a debt, being in the red

explanation.surface: Letters written in red ink.
explanation.definitionFit: A written acknowledgement of a debt, so the letters of someone in the red.

clue.text: High-fliers who make jokes in gym?

parts.note: PE, physical education, is school gym
wits are people who make jokes

explanation.surface: Jokers in a school gymnasium as acrobats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is only a link; the clue reads as jokers in a school gym, but the answer is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapwings, birds named for their cry, which fly in tumbling displays.

clue.text: Newt seen in border is 20 September 2008

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Newt seen in border is 20 September 2008', is garbled: the blog gives EFT (newt) in LIST (border), but the definition after 'is' is lost to a date.
annotationWithheld.clue: Newt seen in border is 20 September 2008
